title: Assignability, subtyping, and excess property checks
hook: TypeScript decides whether one type can stand in for another using structural rules — if the shape fits, the assignment works.

blocks.text: **Assignability** asks whether Source can be used where Target is expected. TypeScript uses **structural subtyping** — Source is assignable if it has at least all properties Target requires with compatible types. This differs from C#'s **nominal** system. **Excess property checks** apply to fresh object literals: extra properties cause errors even when structural rules would otherwise allow them.

entries.plainDefinition: Compatibility based on shape, not declared names.
entries.example: `{ name: string; age: number }` assignable to `{ name: string }`.

entries.plainDefinition: Fresh object literals cannot include undeclared properties.
A newly written `{ ... }` subject to stricter excess property rules.
entries.example: Assign through a variable to bypass — usually a code smell.

blocks.text: Union assignability is directional — `"a"` fits `string` but not reverse. Excess property checks catch typos in config objects. For C# developers, structural typing is the biggest mental model shift.

blocks.title: Variable vs literal
blocks.body: Excess checks apply to fresh literals, not variables already typed wider.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming C# nominal rules apply. Smuggling typos through intermediate variables. Expecting bidirectional union assignability.

blocks.text: strictFunctionTypes makes parameters contravariant. Branding restores nominal-like safety. Optional vs undefined differs under exactOptionalPropertyTypes.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected
blocks.body: Calling TypeScript nominal. Reversing union assignability. Unaware readonly covariance rules.

interviewTakeaways: Structural subtyping — compatible shape means assignable.
Excess property checks on fresh literals only.
60s: TS asks 'does shape fit?' C# asks 'is it declared?' Excess checks catch literal typos.
